articles.title: Improved assessment of Alaskan Arctic coastal wave exposure accounting for landfast ice
articles.titleEn: Improved assessment of Alaskan Arctic coastal wave exposure accounting for landfast ice
articles.abstract: Simulations of the ocean wave climate are critical for assessment of coastal processes and hazards in observation sparse regions such as the Arctic. While the multidecade wind and ice datasets necessary for driving long-term wave simulations have proven reliable for such efforts, the presence of landfast ice along shorelines at scales not represented by these data has been a persistent uncertainty impeding accurate analysis of impacts to Arctic coasts. Here, we explore this uncertainty by producing a historical high-resolution wave simulation and combining simulation outputs with landfast ice data for the Alaskan Arctic. The resulting dataset yields an improved assessment of coastal waves and identifies stark contrasts in the seasonal wave exposure of the Chukchi and Beaufort regions. Notably, analysis shows that absent supplemented landfast ice, coastal ice cover is broadly underestimated by 10 to 25 d, resulting in wave energy being overestimated by 5 to 10% in shallow depths nearshore. Notably, these figures can reach up to 70 d of underestimation for ice cover and 48% overestimation of wave energy in certain locations. The persistent overestimation and potential for extreme positive biases in coastal wave assessment highlight the need for representation of landfast ice in Arctic coastal analysis efforts and our analysis reveals the spatial and temporal biases for related research.

articles.title: Multidimensional vulnerabilities of informal settlements in the Urban South
articles.titleEn: Multidimensional vulnerabilities of informal settlements in the Urban South
articles.abstract: Informal settlements are widespread and rapidly growing, often associated with high vulnerabilities. However, global-scale understanding on their spatial distribution and complexity of vulnerability is limited. Here, we delineate the informal settlements across a sample of 1,914 cities of the Global South by integrating Sentinel-2 imagery with deep learning models, and we explore the heterogeneity of vulnerability using Urban Informal Settlement Vulnerability Index that encompasses living conditions, social infrastructure, and environmental risk. We found that Urban Informal Settlements cover 12.94 ± 2.52% of their total urban areas (approximately 34.04 × 10 3 km 2 ), especially in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Middle Asia. Sub-Saharan African cities have the highest vulnerability of informal settlements, with 31.75 ± 6.20% of total urban areas being occupied by informal settlements, while East Asian cities exhibit relatively low vulnerability across all dimensions. We also find that urban informal settlements with high environmental exposure are widespread in the Global South, and there is a significantly polarized distribution between “low” and “high” vulnerability categories. The findings highlight the disparate distribution of multidimensional vulnerability in informal settlements across the Urban South, providing a comparative evidence base for further local assessment and context-specific policy discussions related to SDG 11.

articles.title: Multiyear dual-isotope fingerprinting at South Asian receptor sites constrains carbon monoxide sources and enhanced oxidation
articles.titleEn: Multiyear dual-isotope fingerprinting at South Asian receptor sites constrains carbon monoxide sources and enhanced oxidation
articles.abstract: Carbon monoxide (CO) is an indirect short-lived climate forcer with uncertainties both in sources and its role in atmospheric oxidation. Based on nine winter-long dual-isotope campaigns at two South Asian receptor sites intercepting the continental outflow, we quantified CO source contributions and emission–sink dynamics. Combustion accounts for 68 to 74% of South Asia regional CO (including 34 to 37% from biomass burning) with secondary atmospheric oxidation contributing 26 to 32% (dominated by oxidation of nonmethane volatile organic compounds (NMVOCs) at 21 to 26%, with methane oxidation contributing 5.5 to 6.4%). These isotope-observational constraints suggest a twice higher role for atmospheric oxidation than in model estimates. Spatially, the absolute contributions of both primary and secondary CO decrease from the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the northern Indian Ocean, while the relative contribution of oxidation-derived CO increases, indicating enhanced secondary CO production near source regions. Observation-model comparison suggests that transport from the continental areas dominates CO over adjacent oceanic regions, with minor local production. During the COVID-19 emission perturbation, combustion-derived CO fell sharply in absolute terms, NMVOC-derived CO rose, and CH 4 -derived CO remained stable, providing an observational constraint on the sensitivity of atmospheric oxidation to emission changes. Our results reveal a significant contribution of CO from atmospheric oxidation in South Asia, calling for a reassessment of regional emission–oxidation coupling in models and of mitigation strategies.

articles.title: Antiferromagnetism and tightly bound Cooper pairs induced by kinetic frustration
articles.titleEn: Antiferromagnetism and tightly bound Cooper pairs induced by kinetic frustration
articles.abstract: Antiferromagnetism and superconductivity are often viewed as competing orders in correlated electron systems. Here, we demonstrate that kinetic frustration in hole motion facilitates their coexistence within the square-lattice repulsive Hubbard model. Combining exact analytical solutions on tailored geometries with large-scale numerical simulations, we reveal a robust pairing mechanism: Holes on opposite sublattices behave as if they carry opposite effective charges due to spin singlet formation from kinetic frustration. This emergent property suppresses phase separation and fosters a coherent d -wave superconducting channel embedded within a long-range antiferromagnetic background. Our findings establish a minimal yet broadly applicable framework for stabilizing strong-coupling superconductivity in doped Mott insulators.

articles.title: Structural insights into the coupling mechanism of vectorial CO 2 uptake by DAB1
articles.titleEn: Structural insights into the coupling mechanism of vectorial CO 2 uptake by DAB1
articles.abstract: CO 2 transporters enable bacterial CO 2 -concentrating mechanisms by catalyzing directional hydration of CO 2 , yet the basis of this vectorial carbonic anhydrase (CA) activity remains an open question. We used cryoelectron microscopy to determine the structure of the DAB1 complex from Thermocrinis albus to 2.29 Å, revealing a heterotrimer in which a deeply buried β-CA active site in DabA is structurally coupled to the proton-translocating subunit DabB. Two conformational states define distinct solvent channels for substrate entry and product exit. A suppressor screen identifies mutations that disrupt coupling while retaining CA activity, underlying the importance of conserved residues that link proton translocation to active-site remodeling. These results support a model in which proton-driven conformational changes regulate substrate access to the active site, enabling vectorial CO 2 hydration.

articles.title: Thermodynamic origin of atmospheric new particle formation: Theory for stable nucleating pairs
articles.titleEn: Thermodynamic origin of atmospheric new particle formation: Theory for stable nucleating pairs
articles.abstract: Atmospheric new particle formation (NPF) has been observed across virtually all tropospheric environments, yet the meteorological conditions that favor or suppress it have resisted clear theoretical resolution. Here we show that, for neutral chemistries in which a strongly bound molecular pair constitutes the critical cluster, the thermodynamic precondition for NPF is set by a single quantity: the effective binding free energy of that pair, Δ G AB ° ( T , RH ) , which captures the competing influences of temperature and relative humidity in a closed-form analytical framework. Applied to the sulfuric acid–dimethylamine system in the boundary layer, the theory reproduces observed clustering across laboratory experiments and field campaigns spanning a polluted megacity, a remote high-altitude site, and an ultra-pristine boreal peatland, all without kinetic fitting parameters; precursor concentrations and the condensation sink enter as separable factors that govern the subsequent production rate. The framework reveals an optimal Δ G AB ° that maximizes cluster production, providing a thermodynamic basis for why NPF peaks at midday, favors spring over other seasons, occurs under heat wave conditions despite temperatures approaching + 40 ° C, and can even arise on rare evenings in near-pristine conditions. More broadly, the theory exposes the inherent relationship between atmospheric conditions and the earliest steps of particle formation, offering a general interpretive tool that complements and extends what observations and simulations alone cannot provide.

articles.title: AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication
articles.titleEn: AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.

articles.title: Extensive glacier loss in the coterminous United States
articles.titleEn: Extensive glacier loss in the coterminous United States
articles.abstract: Glaciers populate the mountain ranges of the western conterminous United States and despite their importance to alpine hydrology, their area and volume change have never been comprehensively evaluated. Our study shows that since the mid-twentieth century about one-quarter of the glaciers have disappeared and the overall area and volume are reduced by one-third. The pattern of glacier shrinkage suggests most glaciers in the conterminous United States are largely maintained by local topographic influences due to their small size. These results improve our understanding of evolving high alpine hydrology and importance to ecosystem processes.

articles.title: Learning dissipative chaotic dynamics with boundedness guarantees
articles.titleEn: Learning dissipative chaotic dynamics with boundedness guarantees
articles.abstract: Chaotic dynamics, commonly seen in weather systems and fluid turbulence, are characterized by their sensitivity to initial conditions, which makes accurate prediction challenging. Recent approaches have focused on developing data-driven models that attempt to preserve invariant statistics over long horizons since many chaotic systems exhibit dissipative behaviors and ergodicity. Despite the recent progress in such models, they are still often prone to generating unbounded trajectories, leading to invalid statistics evaluation. To address this fundamental challenge, we introduce a modular framework that provides formal guarantees of trajectory boundedness for neural network chaotic dynamics models. Our core contribution is a dissipative projection layer that leverages control-theoretic principles to ensure the learned system is dissipative. Specifically, our framework simultaneously learns a dynamics emulator and an energy-like function, where the latter is used to construct an algebraic dissipative constraint within the projection layer. Furthermore, the learned invariant level set provides an outer estimate for the system’s strange attractor, which is known to be difficult to characterize due to its complex geometry. We demonstrate our model’s ability to produce bounded long-horizon forecasts that preserve invariant statistics for chaotic dynamical systems, including Lorenz 96 and a reduced-order model of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation.

articles.title: Watershed Characteristics Modulate the Global Response of Fractional Evapotranspiration to Wet Climate Extremes
articles.titleEn: Watershed Characteristics Modulate the Global Response of Fractional Evapotranspiration to Wet Climate Extremes
articles.abstract: Intensifying wet extremes under continued warming threaten water security and ecosystem functioning by perturbing land–atmosphere water fluxes. Yet, the watershed‐scale controls on how wet‐event intensity and duration translate into changes in fractional evapotranspiration (fET) remain poorly constrained at global scales. Here, using monthly wet climate extreme indices (CEIs) and fET across ∼986 global watersheds, we quantify CEI–fET coupling and attribute its spatial variability to watershed properties using Random Forest models and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Across event types, soil organic carbon (SOC) and groundwater table depth (GWT) consistently structure coupling regimes, indicating a robust role for soil state and subsurface storage. However, the dominant texture axis differs by extreme type: intensity‐based extremes are most strongly organized by SOC–GWT–clay regimes, consistent with pulse retention and buffering, whereas duration‐based extremes are organized by SOC–GWT–silt regimes and permafrost‐related constraints, consistent with persistence‐driven drainage and saturation sensitivity. Supported SHAP‐transition analysis identifies data‐constrained regime boundaries. Lagged correlations further reveal multi‐timescale behavior: coupling varies at short lags but tends to shift toward negative associations at longer lags, especially for duration‐based extremes. In a permafrost‐limited subset, vegetation state and topography become more prominent predictors, highlighting how cold‐region constraints alter which attributes dominate. Together, these results provide a globally consistent diagnostic framework for identifying watershed regimes where intensifying wet extremes are more likely to yield sustained evapotranspiration responses versus reduced fET sensitivity. By quantifying regime thresholds, the study offers a diagnostic framework that may inform targeted mitigation strategies and policy frameworks, such as IPCC adaptation guidelines.

articles.title: Evaluating the EPICC-Model for regional air quality simulation: a comparative study with CAMx and CMAQ
articles.titleEn: Evaluating the EPICC-Model for regional air quality simulation: a comparative study with CAMx and CMAQ
articles.abstract: This study presents a systematic evaluation of the EPICC-Model developed in China for regional PM 2.5 and MDA8 O 3 simulations against established international models, using WRF meteorological fields and a multi-source integrated emission inventory. Results highlight the strengths of the EPICC-Model in several aspects: it achieves relatively high spatial consistency with measurements for PM 2.5 , with an annual index of agreement (IOA) of 0.80, and accurately captures pollution patterns in heavily polluted North China. It also demonstrates improved performance in simulating summer O 3 peaks, reducing maximum bias by more than 20 µg m −3 ; this performance may be partly associated with its inclusion of heterogeneous HONO formation and particulate nitrate photolysis. The model exhibits the highest hit rate (45.6 %) for MDA8 O 3 pollution events exceeding 160 µg m −3 and successfully reproduces persistent pollution episodes. However, all models share common limitations, including insufficient capability in reproducing heavy pollution episodes, systematic underestimation of SO42-, and uncertainties in SOA-related OC simulations. Future improvements should focus on refining secondary aerosol chemistry and emission inventories and further evaluating the representation of vertical turbulent mixing under stable boundary-layer conditions. This study benchmarks the performance of the EPICC-Model against established chemical transport models (CTMs) and identifies priorities for its further development and regional application.

articles.title: Towards high-fidelity simulations of coastal submesoscale baroclinic instabilities with MPAS–O (vE3SM3.0.0) – Part 2: Realistic experiments
articles.titleEn: Towards high-fidelity simulations of coastal submesoscale baroclinic instabilities with MPAS–O (vE3SM3.0.0) – Part 2: Realistic experiments
articles.abstract: River plumes can strongly influence coastal dynamics but are poorly represented in global ocean models due to stringent resolution requirements. Following the idealized simulations presented in a companion paper (Hinson et al., 2026), this study presents submesoscale-permitting realistic simulations using unprecedented regional refinement with MPAS–O. We assess MPAS–O's ability to represent river plume dynamics by comparing with a validated ROMS configuration focused on the Mississippi–Atchafalaya (M–A) plume in the northern Gulf of Mexico (GoM). The variable-resolution mesh spans 1.4 km in the GoM to 100 km in the Pacific and Indian Oceans. We incorporate several improvements to the representation of river forcing in MPAS–O: the pseudo point source treatment of runoff, river temperature prescribed from air temperature, and passive tracers to track freshwater transport. MPAS–O generates vigorous submesoscales in the open GoM, as quantified by probability density functions of surface relative vorticity and divergence. While the model qualitatively captures the M–A plume's seasonal evolution, it does not realistically reproduce the summer submesoscale eddy field on the Texas–Louisiana shelf. A persistent brackish lens associated with reduced vertical mixing forms and is present throughout the M–A plume. We hypothesize that this arises from interacting parameterization and structural design choices within MPAS–O that affect plume stratification and instability growth under realistic forcing, rather than from deficiencies in numerics. Our results demonstrate MPAS–O's potential for simulating submesoscale processes in the open ocean while highlighting challenges in using regional refinement to model coastal dynamics.

articles.title: EnviFlux (v1.0): a simplified surface flux inversion tool based on four-dimensional variational data assimilation (4D-Var)
articles.titleEn: EnviFlux (v1.0): a simplified surface flux inversion tool based on four-dimensional variational data assimilation (4D-Var)
articles.abstract: This paper introduces EnviFlux, which is a software tool (written in C++) to study the inverse problem of estimating the distribution of fluxes of a trace gas globally at the Earth's surface. This is done using a four-dimensional variational technique, which combines information from (i) synthetic observations of the trace gas spanning a defined time window, (ii) a transport model linking the initial concentration and surface fluxes to predictions of the observations, and (iii) a priori information. The novelty of this system – compared to those that attempt to solve for real data – is in its relative simplicity and low cost, allowing new ideas to be assessed and understood quickly and cheaply. This is in line with many other developments in data assimilation that are often first explored using so-called “toy” systems. Part of this paper is to document this system, which is sufficiently complex to allow assimilation of in situ and total column amount (TCA) observation in arbitrary configurations, and has a flexible background error covariance model, but is simple enough to be run relatively quickly. Another part of this paper uses EnviFlux to explore the effect of model error and observation bias on inferred surface fluxes in two example scenarios and with two observation types, namely surface in situ (SIS) and TCA. The first is a highly idealised case with a flux pair (a localised source and a localised sink), where no a priori information concerning their positions is provided. It is found that model errors in the assimilation can severely affect the inferred flux positions and amounts, but observation biases do not affect the positions, but do affect the amounts. The second scenario is closer to a real-world example of methane flux estimates where an a priori is refined with observations. The effect of model error is less than for the first scenario, but is still evident, and the observation biases affect the flux amounts. In both cases, the SIS observations allow a more accurate estimate of surface flux characteristics than the TCA observations, even though the experiments are setup to allow a fair comparison of the two. The last part of the paper raises some research questions that EnviFlux could help address.

Another part of this paper uses EnviFlux to explore the effect of model error and observation bias on inferred surface fluxes in two example scenarios and with two observation types, namely surface in situ (SIS) and TCA. The first is a highly idealised case with a flux pair (a localised source and a localised sink), where no a priori information concerning their positions is provided. It is found that model errors in the assimilation can severely affect the inferred flux positions and amounts, but observation biases do not affect the positions, but do affect the amounts. The second scenario is closer to a real-world example of methane flux estimates where an a priori is refined with observations. The effect of model error is less than for the first scenario, but is still evident, and the observation biases affect the flux amounts. In both cases, the SIS observations allow a more accurate estimate of surface flux characteristics than the TCA observations, even though the experiments are setup to allow a fair comparison of the two. The last part of the paper raises some research questions that EnviFlux could help address.

articles.title: Improving the CLASSIC (v1.8) snow model to better simulate Arctic snowpacks
articles.titleEn: Improving the CLASSIC (v1.8) snow model to better simulate Arctic snowpacks
articles.abstract: This study enhances the snow model of the Canadian Land Surface Scheme including Biogeochemical Cycles (CLASSIC), with a particular focus on Arctic environments. Key snow model physics improvements include adjustments to the thermal conductivity at the top of the first soil layer, a revised computation of the temperature at the snow–soil interface (hereafter, bottom snow temperature), and the addition of a windless exchange coefficient in sensible heat flux calculations. Arctic-specific adaptations include blowing-snow sublimation losses, a new snow compaction scheme, and snow thermal conductivity parameterization. Evaluations at seven mid-latitude and alpine sites (SnowMIP sites) and three Arctic sites (Bylot Island, Umiujaq, and Trail Valley Creek) show that these enhancements improve the overall simulated snowpack characteristics and soil temperatures across both SnowMIP and Arctic sites. The revised bottom snow temperature yields better agreement between simulated and observed snow and bottom snow temperatures. The new windless exchange coefficient reduced the surface temperature RMSE from 3.50 to 1.93 °C on average across all sites. The improved snow compaction scheme reduces the snow depth biases from 12.0 to 0.1 cm on average across the Arctic sites and improves the simulated snow densities while not degrading the overall model performance at the SnowMIP sites. Blowing-snow sublimation had a negligible effect at most sites, except at the wind-exposed sites of Umiujaq, Trail Valley Creek, and Senator Beck, decreasing snow depth on average by 2–4 cm. Adding a new snow thermal conductivity parameterization – combined with all previous developments – reduces the RMSE of the simulated soil temperatures from 5.3 to 3.0 °C on average at all Arctic sites. Our new developments demonstrate the ability of a single-layer snow model to reasonably reproduce Arctic bulk snowpack characteristics, while maintaining good performance at the SnowMIP sites. Inherent uncertainties remain in the forcing datasets, especially due to the harsh Arctic environment characterized by strong winds, snow redistribution, frost, and polar night. Future model developments will focus on spatial-scale simulations across the whole Arctic, with particular attention to snow cover fraction parameterizations to better capture sub-grid-scale spatial heterogeneity in Arctic environments.

articles.title: Process-based evaluation of green roof models for assessment of heat mitigation efficacy in WRF (v4.3.1) and EnergyPlus (v8.6.0)
articles.titleEn: Process-based evaluation of green roof models for assessment of heat mitigation efficacy in WRF (v4.3.1) and EnergyPlus (v8.6.0)
articles.abstract: Green roofs mitigate urban heat, but to fully assess their impact, green roof models must be integrated into urban climate models, where they provide critical surface boundary conditions. Ensuring their reliability requires evaluation, yet such efforts remain limited in the literature. This study addresses that gap by evaluating two configurations of EcoRoof, the green roof module from EnergyPlus (ER o for the original version of the model, and ER m for a modified version), and a multilayer green roof parametrization for WRF (WRF-MLGR) (Heusinger et al., 2018; Sailor, 2008; Zonato et al., 2021). These models were tested against field observations from a monitored green roof in London, Ontario, focusing on latent heat flux ( Q e ), surface temperature ( T surf ), soil heat flux ( Q g ) and substrate water content (SWC). Model performance varied by variable. The two EcoRoof versions showed similar performance, with mean RMSE across study periods of approximately 56–60 W m −2 for Q e , 3–4 °C for T surf , 22 W m −2 for Q g , and 0.03 m 3 m −3 for SWC. Performance for Q e was comparable across models; however, WRF-MLGR exhibited much larger errors for Q g (with mean RMSE exceeding 100 W m −2 ) and SWC (0.06 m 3 m −3 ), along with higher T surf deviations (∼5 °C). Overall, EcoRoof provided a more consistent representation of the daytime energy balance, whereas WRF-MLGR showed structural biases in surface heating. These findings highlight the importance of process-level evaluation for urban climate applications and underscore the need for continued model development to address the structural limitations in green roof parametrizations.

articles.title: MONKI: a three-dimensional Monte Carlo simulator for transfer of polarised light in planetary atmospheres
articles.titleEn: MONKI: a three-dimensional Monte Carlo simulator for transfer of polarised light in planetary atmospheres
articles.abstract: Spectropolarimetry is a powerful tool for characterising planetary atmospheres and surfaces. For the design and operation of spectro(polari)metric instrumentation, numerically simulated signals of the measured radiation are essential. We present MONKI (Monte Carlo KNMI), an efficient and accurate Monte Carlo radiative transfer code written in Fortran. MONKI computes total, linearly polarised, and circularly polarised radiances reflected by and transmitted through planetary atmospheres, fully accounting for the polarisation of light in all orders of scattering. Unlike classical Monte Carlo approaches that rely on post-sampling weight corrections and can therefore produce rare but disproportionately large photon weights, MONKI samples scattering directions from the full polarisation-dependent distribution, consistently in both forward and backward Monte Carlo modes. We provide the corresponding theoretical framework in the appendices. Because of this exact polarised sampling approach, the code converges robustly for optically thick and/or strongly polarising atmospheres. MONKI can handle horizontally homogeneous atmospheres as well as atmospheres with horizontal inhomogeneities, such as three-dimensional (3D) patchy clouds. We validate MONKI through comparisons with other radiative transfer codes. Finally, we present sample simulations of sunlight reflected by the Earth and Venus, and explain the total and polarised radiance features by analysing the altitudes at which photons are scattered. We conclude that MONKI is a versatile and accurate tool for simulations and detailed analyses of total and polarised light emerging from the atmospheres of the Earth, Venus, and, in principle, any other planet.

articles.title: From paper to proof: revealing Congo Basin warming through rescued climate archives
articles.titleEn: From paper to proof: revealing Congo Basin warming through rescued climate archives
articles.abstract: The Congo Basin in Central Africa remains one of the few regions globally where the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has neither assessed changes in hot extremes and extreme precipitation since the 1950s nor attributed such changes to anthropogenic influences, primarily due to the sparsity of in situ observational data. Although extensive daily weather records exist, spanning from the 1900s to the early 2000s and covering numerous stations across the basin, the majority of these remain archived on paper, limiting their accessibility for climate analysis. Here we present and analyse over 1 million temperature and precipitation observations from 37 weather stations in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which have until now been unavailable to the research community. To produce this dataset, we first digitized (imaged) 9885 paper sheets stored in local archives during two dedicated field campaigns. We subsequently apply an improved version of the MeteoSaver software (version 1.1) to transcribe the imaged sheets, yielding daily time series of maximum, minimum, and average temperatures, precipitation, as well as dry bulb and wet bulb temperatures measured at three times per day (06:00, 15:00, and 18:00 local time). After quality control, analysis of multi-decadal temperature data across the basin reveals a consistent and accelerating warming signal since the 1960s, characterized by a warming shift in the distribution of daily maximum, minimum, and average temperatures with each successive decade. Median trends across 21 of the 37 stations with sufficient data availability are 0.22, 0.10, and 0.15 °C per decade for daily maximum, minimum, and average temperatures, respectively, corresponding to approximately 0.7, 0.3, and 0.5 °C of warming during the 1961–1990 period. We further find an increasing frequency of hot extremes and a decreasing frequency of cold extremes with each successive decade, with the most recent decade exhibiting nearly twice as many hot days per year and fewer cold days compared to the earliest decade. Analysis of precipitation at three stations with sufficient data indicates an increased frequency of heavy precipitation events at two stations and no substantial change at the third; however, limited spatial coverage due to data availability restricts broader conclusions for the DRC. Overall, this analysis of rescued weather data from Central Africa highlights the urgent need to close the knowledge gap on climate trends in the Congo Basin, one of the world's most data-sparse yet climatically significant regions.

articles.title: The OpenSat4Weather dataset: Ku-band satellite link data for precipitation monitoring
articles.titleEn: The OpenSat4Weather dataset: Ku-band satellite link data for precipitation monitoring
articles.abstract: The TV-SAT signals received by the ground antennas of Satellite Microwave Links (SMLs) can be opportunistically used for detecting and quantifying precipitation. Consequently, SMLs have the potential to serve as low-cost rainfall sensors complementing conventional instruments. However, a major challenge for opportunistic sensors, including both SMLs and their terrestrial counterpart – Commercial Microwave Links (CMLs) – is related to data ownership and accessibility constraints, possibly hindering progress in the development of processing tools and validation studies. This limitation highlights the importance of openly accessible datasets. While CML open datasets are already available, there are no large-scale SML datasets in public repositories. To address this gap, we introduce the OpenSat4Weather dataset, a comprehensive and openly accessible collection of measurements from 215 SML sensors deployed in Southern France, over a five-month period from August to December 2022. The dataset is accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16530166 (Nebuloni et al., 2025b). OpenSat4Weather also includes concurrent conventional measurements, namely, 6 min rainfall depths from 113 operational rain gauges, and radar-based estimates of rainfall intensity along each SML path. The radar data were derived from the gauge-adjusted weather radar product PANTHERE provided by Météo-France. Additionally, the dataset stores ERA5 reanalysis data of the 0 °C isotherm height for rain height estimation, which are essential for accurately converting the received signal level into rainfall intensity. In this paper, we detail the OpenSat4Weather data preparation process and draw statistics of data availability. We then provide a descriptive analysis of the dataset, including rainfall characteristics, derived from rain gauges, statistical properties of the SML received signal levels, and a comparison between SML and radar data. In addition, we illustrate examples of disturbances and anomalous patterns observed in raw SML signals. Finally, we provide some practical guidelines for processing and analyzing SML data. Our ultimate goal is to promote open research initiatives aimed at accelerating the development of SML-based applications. Enhancing rainfall monitoring by opportunistic sensors has the potential to provide substantial benefits, particularly in regions where conventional networks are sparse or unavailable.

articles.title: Phenological Flexibility in Nesting Grassland Birds Over a Half Century Informs Timing of Management
articles.titleEn: Phenological Flexibility in Nesting Grassland Birds Over a Half Century Informs Timing of Management
articles.abstract: The timing of biological events for wildlife species reflects and influences ecological and evolutionary processes and helps guide management actions to meet conservation objectives. Climate change may cause phenological shifts across trophic levels and ecosystems, which can have broad ecological impacts. Shifts may also result in mistiming between management practices based on historical conditions and current biological events, reducing the effectiveness of natural resource management and conservation efforts. We analyzed nesting phenology patterns over recent decades across North America for 44 species of grassland‐nesting birds, including waterfowl, upland gamebirds, shorebirds, and passerines, many of which have experienced precipitous population declines. Understanding nesting phenologies of these species is important to their conservation, as grassland management activities often conflict with reproductive periods leading to high nest and young mortality. We compiled a dataset of over 172,000 nest records spanning five decades and evaluated environmental factors influencing long‐term shifts and short‐term flexibility in nesting phenology. We found considerable variation in responses among species, with differences in both direction and magnitude of spatiotemporal effects on nest initiation dates. Notably, the community‐level nesting season lengthened over time, but shifts exhibited spatial heterogeneity within this community of grassland birds. Nesting dates shifted asymmetrically across the breeding season with differential changes in early, peak, and late nesting dates whereas long‐term changes were mediated by weather and geographic gradients. For example, nest initiation was earlier in warmer and wetter years. By applying a quantile‐based analysis, we provide estimates of the full nesting period that could serve as a flexible tool for scheduling monitoring efforts and balancing management and human activities with periods of reduced nesting activity. Our collaborative effort illustrates the challenges and opportunities of collecting long‐term data on avian communities necessary for answering questions across large regions but highlights the value of research coordination for bird conservation.

articles.title: What matters when? Temporal development of drivers and sources of nitrous oxide emissions in winter wheat
articles.titleEn: What matters when? Temporal development of drivers and sources of nitrous oxide emissions in winter wheat
articles.abstract: Agriculture is the largest anthropogenic source of nitrous oxide (N 2 O), primarily due to nitrogen (N) fertilization. Understanding how the influence of key drivers and the relative contribution of source processes change throughout cropping seasons is crucial for developing effective strategies to mitigate N 2 O emissions. In this study, we combined high-resolution eddy covariance (EC) flux measurements and explainable machine learning (ML) across the 2022–2023 winter wheat season and the subsequent summer cover crop at a temperate site in Switzerland, complemented by stable isotope analyses conducted in March 2023 following a fertilization event. We used Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to interpret an XGBoost model trained to predict N 2 O fluxes, enabling a time-resolved assessment of driver contributions. Crop establishment and early spring emerged as particularly vulnerable periods, characterized by mismatches between N supply and plant demand that led to surplus soil mineral N and elevated N 2 O fluxes under favorable moisture and temperature conditions. Elevated gross primary productivity (GPP, used as a proxy for crop activity and N demand) showed a consistent negative effect on N 2 O fluxes, supporting the role of active vegetation as a competing N sink. Stable isotope source partitioning identified denitrification as the dominant N 2 O production pathway during the early-spring post-fertilization period, consistent with poor soil drainage and high soil moisture. Cumulative N 2 O emissions over the nine-month winter wheat season reached 5.5 kg N 2 O-N ha −1 , with yield-scaled emissions of 1.1 kg N 2 O-N Mg −1 grain, both values exceeding those typically reported for wheat. Our findings highlight the value of combining EC, explainable ML, and stable isotope approaches to resolve the temporal dynamics of N 2 O emissions and identify vulnerable windows for targeted mitigation in cropping systems.

articles.title: Linking marine benthic biodiversity and ecosystem functions related to carbon cycling in a continental mud depocenter
articles.titleEn: Linking marine benthic biodiversity and ecosystem functions related to carbon cycling in a continental mud depocenter
articles.abstract: The importance of carbon storage in continental seafloor sediments is increasingly recognized, yet the role of benthic macrofaunal biodiversity in the regulation of these processes remains poorly understood. Benthic macrofauna contributes to organic carbon cycling through respiration and secondary production, while sediment reworking (bioturbation) and ventilation (bioirrigation) by infauna promote the redistribution and remineralization of organic matter in sediments. Here, we investigated how benthic community structure, functional traits, and the relationship between biodiversity and calculated potential ecosystem functioning related to carbon cycling vary along environmental gradients in muddy sediments of the southeastern North Sea. Based on 171 macrofaunal taxa collected from 50 stations, hierarchical clustering based on abundance data categorized the macrofaunal communities into four distinct structural groups. Distance-based redundancy analysis (dbRDA) revealed that community functional composition was primarily structured by bottom hydrodynamics (salinity and bottom shear stress) and sediment characteristics (sorting, skewness, kurtosis, and D50). Biomass-weighted functional trait vectors, mapped onto a non-metric multidimensional scaling (nMDS) space, showed a clear structural shift with communities in the deep clusters being dominated by mobile biodiffusors and subsurface filter feeders, whereas shallow clusters were characterized by less mobile, surface-modifying bivalves and polychaetes. These contrasting patterns led to pronounced differences in calculated potential ecosystem functioning: bioturbation and bioirrigation potentials were significantly higher in deeper communities, whereas the calculated community secondary production and respiration were higher in shallow communities. Across all stations, community secondary production and respiration increased with taxonomic and functional richness, while bioturbation and bioirrigation potentials were negatively related to biodiversity and community evenness. Interaction regressions and simple slope analyses revealed that environmental gradients significantly modulated the biodiversity–ecosystem functioning (BEF) relationships. Our findings demonstrate that environmental gradients fundamentally shape both benthic community structure and the link between biodiversity and essential ecosystem functions related to carbon dynamics in fine-grained sediment and organic matter in shelf sea systems.

articles.title: Human-centred design approaches to tsunami mitigation under sea level rise in Kesennuma, Japan
articles.titleEn: Human-centred design approaches to tsunami mitigation under sea level rise in Kesennuma, Japan
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Human-centred design (HCD) is increasingly prioritised as studies show human experience is critical in infrastructure use, and recent policies call for more socially responsive design. Tsunami impacts intensify as sea level rise (SLR) raises baseline water levels and reduces existing defence effectiveness. This study aims to develop and evaluate HCD-integrated multi-layered tsunami defences, assessing whether socially integrated designs can deliver effective protection under projected SLR conditions. Based on identified infrastructure preferences in Kesennuma City, Japan, we develop three multi-layered defence configurations: an environmentally integrated eco-hybrid system (Defence 1), a discreet open-feeling barrier system (Defence 2), and a reinforced high-performance system (Defence 3). Using TUNAMI-N2 numerical modelling, 150 simulations combine three tsunami sources, five SLR conditions, and five defence states. Results for inundation extent, fatality rates, and economic loss show a consistent hierarchy: Defence 3 achieves the strongest containment, while Defence 2, which more closely aligns with residents' preferences for openness and access, delivers near equivalent reductions typically within 10 %–15 %. Defence 1 provides only limited hazard reduction and is unsuitable as a standalone mitigation system. We show that HCD-integrated configurations can deliver strong technical performance and support a shift toward socially integrated, multi-layered tsunami protection under rising sea levels.
articles.abstractEn: Human-centred design (HCD) is increasingly prioritised as studies show human experience is critical in infrastructure use, and recent policies call for more socially responsive design. Tsunami impacts intensify as sea level rise (SLR) raises baseline water levels and reduces existing defence effectiveness. This study aims to develop and evaluate HCD-integrated multi-layered tsunami defences, assessing whether socially integrated designs can deliver effective protection under projected SLR conditions. Based on identified infrastructure preferences in Kesennuma City, Japan, we develop three multi-layered defence configurations: an environmentally integrated eco-hybrid system (Defence 1), a discreet open-feeling barrier system (Defence 2), and a reinforced high-performance system (Defence 3). Using TUNAMI-N2 numerical modelling, 150 simulations combine three tsunami sources, five SLR conditions, and five defence states. Results for inundation extent, fatality rates, and economic loss show a consistent hierarchy: Defence 3 achieves the strongest containment, while Defence 2, which more closely aligns with residents' preferences for openness and access, delivers near equivalent reductions typically within 10 %–15 %. Defence 1 provides only limited hazard reduction and is unsuitable as a standalone mitigation system. We show that HCD-integrated configurations can deliver strong technical performance and support a shift toward socially integrated, multi-layered tsunami protection under rising sea levels.

articles.title: Anomalous spin–lattice coupling in a 2D antiferromagnetic semiconductor revealed by surface acoustic Rayleigh waves
articles.titleEn: Anomalous spin–lattice coupling in a 2D antiferromagnetic semiconductor revealed by surface acoustic Rayleigh waves
articles.abstract: Magnetic order in van der Waals magnets can strongly influence their lattice dynamics, yet how it affects local and macroscopic manifestations of spin-phonon coupling remains unclear. Optical phonons probe bond-scale exchange modulation and short-range spin correlations, whereas long-wavelength acoustic modes couple to uniform strain fields and are sensitive to renormalization of the macroscopic elastic tensor associated with long-range magnetic order. Experimentally accessing these acoustic excitations in low-dimensional crystals is challenging due to their low energies and the small lateral dimensions of exfoliated samples. Here, we employ Brillouin–Mandelstam scattering spectroscopy to investigate surface acoustic phonons in exfoliated NiPS 3 thin films across the antiferromagnetic transition. Our results show a single Rayleigh surface mode whose phase velocity decreases significantly across the Néel temperature. This anomaly reflects a strong magnetoelastic renormalization of the elastic constants triggered by the onset of antiferromagnetic order. First-principles calculations, combined with continuum finite-element modeling reproduce the Rayleigh-wave dispersion and its magnetic-order–induced shift. The results reveal how microscopic exchange interactions govern the macroscopic elastic response of two-dimensional antiferromagnetic semiconductors, enabling magnetically tunable phononic, magnonic, and strain-mediated spintronic devices.

articles.title: Interpretable AI-guided discovery of degradable ionizable lipids with enhanced hepatic mRNA delivery in vivo
articles.titleEn: Interpretable AI-guided discovery of degradable ionizable lipids with enhanced hepatic mRNA delivery in vivo
articles.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) enable RNA medicines, yet ionizable-lipid discovery remains largely empirical, particularly when in vitro activity must be translated into functional hepatic delivery in vivo. Here we establish an interpretable discovery framework that combines modular degradable lipid chemistry, high-throughput phenotyping, machine learning, virtual library expansion, and independent in vivo validation to define a learnable ionizable-lipid design space. Starting from a 520-member library, we train an XGBoost model on firefly luciferase (Fluc) expression in HeLa cells and use physicochemical descriptors and molecular fingerprints to prospectively prioritize candidates with higher predicted in vitro transfection activity across a 10,920-member virtual space. In vivo phenotyping subsequently identifies PA97MD101 as a lead ionizable lipid. In mice, PA97MD101 enhances hepatic mRNA expression and Cre-dependent recombination and supports Cas9/sgTtr-mediated TTR suppression. Its performance is associated with pH-dependent membrane activity and reduced lysosomal colocalization. These findings support further evaluation of PA97MD101 for functional hepatic RNA delivery.

articles.title: Ki-67, the chromosome periphery and de-compartmentalisation each contribute to nucleophosmin mislocalisation in acute myeloid leukaemia
articles.titleEn: Ki-67, the chromosome periphery and de-compartmentalisation each contribute to nucleophosmin mislocalisation in acute myeloid leukaemia
articles.abstract: The mitotic chromosome periphery (MCP) is an important chromosome compartment but links to disease remains elusive. Here we define the mitosis-specific, Ki-67 interactome, identifying additional MCP components and revealing that MCP genes are commonly mutated in cancer, including nucleophosmin (NPM1). Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML)-specific NPM1 mutations (NPM1c + ), result in protein mislocalisation (nucleolus to cytoplasm). We demonstrate that NPM1c+ fails to adequately bind to the MCP, instead forming aggregates during mitosis. We also report that, de-compartmentalisation at mitotic onset allows formation of NPM1wt/c+ multimers. These mislocalisation mechanisms contribute to a significant hinderance of NPM1 re-entry into daughter cell nucleoli. Enhancing MCP loading capacity via Ki-67 overexpression resulted in increased MCP-bound NPM1c+ during mitosis and greater yield of nucleolar NPM1c + . Ki-67 expression demonstrated a significant interaction with NPM1 mutation status on AML patient overall survival, whereby higher Ki-67 was associated with increased hazard in NPM1wt but reduced hazard in NPM1c+ patients. This work reveals mechanistic insight into AML and evidence that the MCP has untapped therapeutic potential.

articles.title: Block-fitness modeling of the global air mobility network
articles.titleEn: Block-fitness modeling of the global air mobility network
articles.abstract: Accurate representations of origin-destination (OD) passenger flows on the World Air Transportation Network (WAN) are fundamental inputs to models of global mobility, epidemic risk, and infrastructure planning. However, OD data are largely commercial and proprietary, therefore often inaccessible to the research community. Here we introduce a generative model that treats air mobility as a stochastic process within a sparse maximum-entropy framework, informed by aggregate traffic volumes of individual locations and geographic regions. The model accurately reconstructs both network structure and mobility flows, yielding epidemic spreading trajectories that closely match those obtained using real mobility data. Furthermore, the method can be effectively implemented using open data on flight routes and airport traffic, reducing dependence on proprietary datasets. Our approach provides a scalable, interpretable, and computationally efficient framework for scenario analysis and policy design in global mobility systems.

articles.title: Sea-level contribution from Thwaites Glacier doubles in an observation-constrained ice-sheet model
articles.titleEn: Sea-level contribution from Thwaites Glacier doubles in an observation-constrained ice-sheet model
articles.abstract: Thwaites Glacier is a major contributor to Antarctic mass loss and a key source of uncertainty in future sea-level rise. Ocean-driven melting at its grounding line drives rapid retreat, yet most models treat the transition between grounded and floating ice as a sharp boundary, neglecting kilometer-scale seawater intrusions that develop as the grounding line migrates and forms a grounding zone. Here, we show that actively-melting grounding zones are required to reproduce nearly three decades of observed retreat, thinning, and acceleration of Thwaites Glacier in a calibrated ice-sheet model, with successful reconstruction occurring only when grounding zones are represented as 2-5 km wide regions. Extending this model forward, we show that grounding-zone processes govern glacier’s detachment from stabilizing seafloor ridges, enabling unpinning as early as 2038 and producing up to 30 ± 6 mm of global mean sea-level rise by 2100 - approximately double previous projections even without additional climate warming.

articles.title: Precision functional mapping of imagined and experienced pain
articles.titleEn: Precision functional mapping of imagined and experienced pain
articles.abstract: Imagination is a principal human capacity, enabling simulation of sensations and situations for planning, learning, and empathy. We examined neural representations of experienced and imagined pain across eight body sites using deep-phenotyping, precision functional MRI with over seven hours of scanning per participant (N = 9). Here we show, using conventional mapping, pattern classification, and representational similarity analyses, that both imagined and experienced pain activated nociceptive regions (e.g., dorsoposterior insula) and non-nociceptive regions (e.g., premotor areas and inferior inter-effector motor cortex). However, imagined pain did not reliably reactivate body site-selective nociceptive patterns in any region. Instead, imagined and experienced pain shared multivariate representations across widespread cortical and subcortical regions, particularly transmodal cortical areas including dorsomedial and lateral prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and thalamus. These findings suggest that imagination generates distributed pain-like activity, but with separable neural codes for imagined and experienced pain. This distinction may explain the difficulty of vividly imagining pain and clarify its potential roles in empathy, planning, and pain chronification.

articles.title: Genomic bases of short-term evolution in wild barn owls revealed by long-term monitoring and population-scale sequencing
articles.titleEn: Genomic bases of short-term evolution in wild barn owls revealed by long-term monitoring and population-scale sequencing
articles.abstract: Understanding how wild populations undergo rapid phenotypic evolution requires linking phenotypic change to its underlying genomic architecture over contemporary timescales. Here, we leverage a 30-year study of Swiss barn owls ( Tyto alba ) to examine long-term changes in two melanin-based traits (plumage coloration and spottiness) that have previously been linked to multiple fitness-related traits. We document a consistent temporal shift toward darker and more heavily spotted individuals and show, using whole-genome sequencing of 3,102 individuals, that these traits are controlled by a small number of loci of major effect with partially overlapping architectures. Temporal allele frequency analyses reveal subtle but consistent changes at these loci. By comparing empirical trajectories to simulations, we show that genetic drift alone is insufficient to explain the observed patterns at one major locus, indicating a role for selection. Our results demonstrate how selection acting on a small number of loci can contribute to rapid phenotypic evolution of continuous traits in the wild and highlight the value of long-term genomic and phenotypic monitoring for disentangling evolutionary processes.

articles.title: Continuous-time noise mitigation in analogue quantum simulation
articles.titleEn: Continuous-time noise mitigation in analogue quantum simulation
articles.abstract: Analogue quantum simulators offer a promising route to explore quantum many-body dynamics beyond classical reach in the near term. However, their vulnerability to noise limits the accuracy of simulations. Here, we establish a continuous-time framework for mitigating noise in analogue quantum simulation. Our protocol fully preserves the continuous-time nature by avoiding any active control or measurement of the system during the dynamics, while achieving exact noise cancellation. This requires a small number of ancillary qubits, whose interaction with the system, combined with classical post-processing of joint measurement data, is tailored to cancel the effect of noise. Furthermore, the protocol is Hamiltonian-independent and robust to realistic ancilla noise. This work points to a promising direction for achieving high-fidelity analogue quantum simulation in the presence of noise.

articles.title: Fingerprint Evidence for Human Effects on Climate: Advances After the 2009 Endangerment Finding
articles.titleEn: Fingerprint Evidence for Human Effects on Climate: Advances After the 2009 Endangerment Finding
articles.abstract: Here we briefly review key advances in the field of climate fingerprinting. Fingerprint studies rely on pattern information to identify human and natural influences on Earth's climate. Our focus is on advances after 2009—the date of the finding by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) that emissions of six different greenhouse gases affect Earth's climate and endanger human health and welfare. In contrast to the conclusions from a 2025 review of climate science issued by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), we demonstrate that post‐2009 scientific advances have markedly increased confidence in the identification of significant anthropogenic contributions to global climate change. These advances were enabled by longer and improved observations of climate change, by large single‐model and multi‐model ensembles of simulations that yield estimates of forced climate change signals and natural variability, and by the application of climate fingerprint methods to a wide array of independently monitored variables. Increasingly, scientists are now able to quantify the impact of human‐caused climate change on the probability and intensity of certain types of extreme event, particularly in the case of heat waves and the heavy rainfall in some regions. In tandem with such scientific advances, global warming has also advanced: the post‐2009 period included the 10 warmest years in instrumental surface temperature records, enhancing the signal of human‐caused warming relative to intrinsic variability. The evidence for pervasive human fingerprints throughout Earth's climate system is incontrovertible.

articles.title: A Catchment‐Based Global Model of River Discharge and Flow Velocity for Earth System Models
articles.titleEn: A Catchment‐Based Global Model of River Discharge and Flow Velocity for Earth System Models
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: The representation of river flows in Earth System Models (ESMs) is crucial for understanding water resources availability, contaminant transport, and the impacts of climate change on river systems. In this study, we introduce a global runoff routing model founded on hydraulic geometry principles and hydrologic catchments, specifically designed for integration with ESMs. To simulate river dynamics, the model capitalizes on (a) the river network topology defined by the Pfafstetter coding system, (b) hydraulic geometry principles that connect river discharge to flow velocity, and (c) calibration using more than 2.7 million intermittent field measurements of flow velocity in the contiguous US (CONUS). The model is shown to produce reasonably accurate natural daily river discharge over CONUS except within some arid regions and the region adjacent to the Great Lakes, where streamflow is strongly impacted by reservoir management and by the natural buffering behavior of the large lakes themselves. The average correlation coefficient for discharge (vs. in situ measurements) is 0.80 for tested major rivers over CONUS except in arid regions and the Great Lakes. A unique feature of the model is its ability to simulate flow velocity with realistic magnitudes, standing it in good stead for tracer tracking and water management applications.

articles.title: Diagnosing Latent Storage Representations in LSTM Reservoir Release Policies
articles.titleEn: Diagnosing Latent Storage Representations in LSTM Reservoir Release Policies
articles.abstract: The influence of reservoirs on the water cycle introduces significant uncertainty for hydrologic prediction. The representation of reservoirs in hydrologic models ideally must be accurate, interpretable, and transferable across sites. Recent studies have highlighted the potential for data‐driven methods, including long short‐term memory (LSTM) networks, to accurately capture reservoir releases. However, the performance of LSTM models of reservoir releases has not yet been diagnosed on a large‐sample data set to understand whether their accuracy is physically justified. This study evaluates the ability of LSTMs to represent reservoir release policies across the continental U.S., leveraging the recently developed ResOpsUS data set. In particular, we focus on whether LSTMs can infer a latent storage representation without being provided observed storage as input. We find that in many cases the LSTM succeeds in encoding physically interpretable storage dynamics in its internal states, despite measurement errors in the data. However, the model accuracy is only weakly related to the strength of the learned storage representation; instead, it is log‐linearly related to the degree of regulation. In addition, LSTMs struggle to generalize storage dynamics and learned policies in space with pooled training. This study contributes to the growing literature on interpreting deep learning models of human‐hydrologic systems.

articles.title: Characteristic‐Aligned Control‐Volume Physics‐Informed Neural Network for Flood‐Wave Propagation and Roughness Estimation
articles.titleEn: Characteristic‐Aligned Control‐Volume Physics‐Informed Neural Network for Flood‐Wave Propagation and Roughness Estimation
articles.abstract: Physics‐informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a promising framework for river hydrodynamic simulation and parameter inversion under sparse observations. However, spatial heterogeneity in channel geometry and roughness causes strong variations in flood‐wave propagation and parameter sensitivity, challenging local conservation and joint state‐parameter estimation. This study proposes a Characteristic‐aligned Control‐volume Physics‐Informed Neural Network for Roughness Estimation (CC‐PINN‐RE). It constructs dynamic diamond‐shaped space‐time control volumes from local characteristic speeds of the Saint‐Venant equations, enforces mass and momentum conservation in integral form, and combines adaptive control‐volume management with local‐sensitivity‐weighted roughness regularization. The method is evaluated on three one‐dimensional channel cases of increasing complexity against strong‐form PINN‐RE and fixed‐control‐volume cvPINN‐RE. CC‐PINN‐RE achieves the lowest errors in eight of nine relative metrics for water depth, discharge, and roughness. In Case 3, where channel width, bed slope, and roughness vary spatially, it reduces the corresponding errors by 57.0%, 82.2%, and 57.3% relative to PINN‐RE and reduces the maximum absolute error in peak water depth by 69.7%. Ablation experiments with three random seeds support the contributions of the three proposed components. Observation‐deployment experiments show that increasing the number of monitoring stations is generally more effective than increasing temporal sampling frequency at individual stations. Under 0%–2% observational noise in Case 3, the model remains stable. These results indicate that CC‐PINN‐RE provides a physically consistent framework for integrating characteristic propagation, local conservation, and parameter inversion, offering a useful basis for joint hydrodynamic reconstruction and spatially varying roughness estimation in heterogeneous river channels.

articles.title: A method quantifying soil melanin to understand fungal impacts on soil carbon stability
articles.titleEn: A method quantifying soil melanin to understand fungal impacts on soil carbon stability
articles.abstract: Fungal necromass, particularly dead microbial cells rich in melanin, is an important contributor to long-term soil carbon stabilization. Progress in understanding the role of soil melanin is limited by the lack of validated analytical methods. DNA-based approaches estimate only the genetic potential for melanin production and therefore provide indirect evidence of melanin occurrence. To directly assess soil melanin, we evaluated spectroscopic and spectrophotometric assays; however, both approaches proved insufficiently specific due to interference from chemically related compounds. Here, we introduce a liquid chromatography method that enables quantification of major fungal melanin types in soils. By enabling direct quantification of fungal melanin in soil, this framework allows longstanding hypotheses regarding melanized fungal necromass and soil carbon stabilization to be tested mechanistically. Here, we show with the proposed method that soil melanin concentrations are strongly correlated with total soil carbon, supporting a central role for fungal melanin in long-term soil carbon stabilization.

articles.title: An Online Moisture Tagging Framework for Detrainment of Convective Hydrometeors and Associated Precipitation in Convection‐Permitting Models
articles.titleEn: An Online Moisture Tagging Framework for Detrainment of Convective Hydrometeors and Associated Precipitation in Convection‐Permitting Models
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Convective detrainment is an important process in mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) that strongly influence adjacent stratiform clouds and precipitation. However, it remains difficult to quantify convective detrainment in numerical models. In this study, we develop an online convection identification and water vapor tracer (WVT) framework based on the Eulerian WVTs coupled with Weather Research and Forecasting convection‐permitting model. Convection is identified using radar reflectivity, and two types of tracers are introduced to track water species and precipitation within convective regions and those detrained from them, which can be distinguished from those newly generated in the stratiform areas. The framework is applied to both an idealized case and a real case. In the idealized simulation, the framework captures the convective detrainment and its associated precipitation during the lifecycle of convective systems featured by rapid evolution in location and structure. In the real case, the framework demonstrates distinct temporal variations in the intensity and area coverage of stratiform precipitation produced by convective detrainment. Both the ice‐ and liquid‐phase detrainments decrease dramatically at the moment when convective precipitation starts to increase, suggesting intensified conversion from cloud to precipitating hydrometeors. After that, the conversion efficiency weakens, which is favorable for the formation of stratiform clouds and precipitation. Overall, this framework provides a useful tool for quantifying the characteristics and impacts of convective detrainment and for evaluating convective parameterization schemes.

articles.title: Quantifying Vegetation Dependence on Groundwater: Evidence From Northern China's Drylands
articles.titleEn: Quantifying Vegetation Dependence on Groundwater: Evidence From Northern China's Drylands
articles.abstract: Groundwater is a critical source for vegetation in drylands, yet the quantification of vegetation dependence on groundwater (VDG) remains underexplored. Understanding this dependence is essential for unraveling vegetation‐groundwater interactions and informing sustainable water resources management in drylands. This study constructed a vegetation response curve to depth to groundwater (DTG) by analyzing the relationship between DTG and the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) at the pixel scale. A new method was developed to quantify VDG from the fitted NDVI–DTG response curve, where VDG was defined as the rate of NDVI change per unit change in normalized DTG at the inflection point of the NDVI–DTG response curve. VDG values were obtained for nine representative arid, semi‐arid, and semi‐humid regions in northern China (with an annual precipitation gradient of 200–800 mm). VDG shows pronounced spatial variation across the nine regions, with mean values decreasing from approximately 1.28 in the driest region to approximately 0.24 in the wettest region along the precipitation gradient. A strong negative correlation between annual precipitation (P) and VDG was identified (VDG = 2.08e −0.0037P ), highlighting precipitation as a dominant regulator of VDG across regions. The research provides new empirical evidence for a deeper understanding of the effects of groundwater on vegetation, and also provides strong scientific support for groundwater management and ecological restoration with various annual precipitation amounts.

articles.title: Spatiotemporal Variability of Water Transit Time Distribution Across an Alpine Stream Network
articles.titleEn: Spatiotemporal Variability of Water Transit Time Distribution Across an Alpine Stream Network
articles.abstract: Water transit time (TT), the time elapsed from its entrance into a catchment and its exit through a stream section, is a useful indicator of catchment transport dynamics. Its distribution (TTD) is typically estimated at a single cross section where tracer data are available. However, spatial variability of TTD is key to understanding how heterogeneous source areas contribute to solute and water quality dynamics. Here, we investigate how TTD varies along a stream network. To this end, we analyzed stable isotopes in rainfall (three stations) and streamwater (eight sampling sites) in the Valfredda network draining an alpine catchment. To quantitatively analyze the data, we developed a spatially explicit model of TTD based on StorAge Selection (SAS) functions. The catchment is discretized into subcatchment units, each characterized by distinct SAS functions. Subcatchment TTDs are routed through the network to estimate TTDs at every cross section. Parameter estimation relies on a hierarchical Bayesian framework, which ensures consistency across subcatchments while allowing heterogeneity. Results indicate that streamflow preferentially samples older water from storage, with only a limited number of flow events triggering young water release. Despite pronounced heterogeneity in geomorphology and land cover, the inferred SAS functions exhibit only mild spatial variability. Differences in TTDs are driven primarily by variations in precipitation phase (liquid vs. solid) and the timing of snowmelt‐driven fluxes, rather than by intrinsic differences in mixing mechanisms. Both sources of variability are explicitly represented within the proposed framework, highlighting its general applicability to reveal transport dynamics at the catchment scale.

articles.title: On the Adversarial Robustness of Hydrological Models
articles.titleEn: On the Adversarial Robustness of Hydrological Models
articles.abstract: The evaluation of hydrological models is essential for both model selection and reliability assessment. However, comparing predictions with observations alone is insufficient to fully characterize model behavior. This limitation is particularly relevant to deep learning (DL) models because of their complex internal structures. In risk‐averse operational settings, water managers require models whose reliability and failure modes have been carefully evaluated because unstable predictions can put critical infrastructure at risk. Motivated by the need to assess model reliability before operational deployment, we introduce and explore adversarial robustness analysis for hydrological modeling and evaluate whether small, targeted perturbations to meteorological forcings induce substantial changes in simulated discharge. We compare a physical‐conceptual model (HBV) with a deep learning‐based model (LSTM) across 1,347 German catchments using perturbations of varying magnitudes generated by the fast gradient sign method (FGSM). We find that FGSM perturbations generally reduce Kling–Gupta efficiency and increase mean squared error. However, widespread catastrophic failures under the specific FGSM perturbations are not observed, and LSTM generally exhibits less performance degradation than HBV. In the examined catchments, changes in the predicted hydrographs and time‐averaged internal model states often vary approximately linearly with perturbation magnitude, providing a compact summary of how errors grow under such perturbations. Similar patterns are observed along random perturbation directions in selected catchments, suggesting that, in those catchments, small input changes produce approximately proportional changes in model output. Overall, these findings characterize local predictive stability under controlled stress tests and motivate future studies of model robustness in real‐world operational settings.

articles.title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Active Root Zone Storage Revealed From Hybrid Machine Learning
articles.titleEn: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Active Root Zone Storage Revealed From Hybrid Machine Learning
articles.abstract: Water within the root zone regulates water, energy, and carbon exchanges at the land‐atmosphere interface, yet the dynamically active portion of subsurface water that ecosystems mobilize for evapotranspiration (ET) remains unclear, because it represents only part of the total subsurface storage. To address this gap, we develop a catchment‐scale, ecosystem‐oriented hybrid machine learning model that integrates a parsimonious ecohydrological structure with data‐driven flexibility to infer time‐varying active root zone storage (a S rz ) as a latent state variable. Without prescribing rooting depth or soil layers, the model learns adaptive water partitioning from multi‐source observations of ET, runoff, snow, and terrestrial water storage, enabling diagnosis of both dynamic a S rz and its realized capacity. Applied across hundreds of U.S. catchments over the period 2001–2020, the framework reveals coherent spatial and hydroclimatic patterns, with a S rz peaking in transitional regions where atmospheric demand and water supply are balanced. The realized capacity reflects how belowground water access varies with long‐term hydroclimatic and substrate constraints. We further show that defining storage as a realized quantity through system dynamics improves stability and interpretability under varying observational and structural conditions. Overall, this study demonstrates how hybrid modeling can be used to diagnose ecosystem‐accessible water storage as a latent state, providing a physically consistent and observation‐informed pathway to quantify belowground processes that remain inaccessible to direct measurement and control key land‐atmosphere interactions.

articles.title: Can Competition‐Based Programs Promote Conservation in Agriculture? Evidence From the “Most Crop per Drop” Contest
articles.titleEn: Can Competition‐Based Programs Promote Conservation in Agriculture? Evidence From the “Most Crop per Drop” Contest
articles.abstract: This paper evaluates the Arkansas “Most Crop per Drop” Irrigation Yield Contest, a novel competition‐based Extension program designed to increase the adoption of Irrigation Water Management (IWM) practices among farmers. We use survey data to classify producers into three categories: contestants, informed non‐participants with some connection to the contest, and uninformed non‐participants with no knowledge of it. Difference‐in‐Differences estimates for years before and after the program indicate that contestants applied IWM practices on about four percentage points more of their irrigated land than non‐participants who were unaware of the contest, with results robust to matching methods and reclassifying non‐contestants based on their proximity to contest fields. Informed non‐participants increased IWM adoption by more than two percentage points relative to uninformed peers, providing evidence of meaningful spillover effects from the contest to a broader group of producers.

articles.title: Physics‐Informed Fusion Learning for Nowcasting Fault Detection of Hydrological Multi Sensor Network
articles.titleEn: Physics‐Informed Fusion Learning for Nowcasting Fault Detection of Hydrological Multi Sensor Network
articles.abstract: Urban flood monitoring demands timely, reliable decisions under urgent and often unseen conditions. However, faults in sensor networks can undermine response, leading to human and economic losses. To address these issues, we propose a Nowcasting Physics‐Informed (NPI) model for fault detection in streamflow sensors, with a 100‐min memory window at 2‐min resolution. A Long Short‐Term Memory (LSTM) consumes fused features from measured signals and Storm Water Management Model simulator outputs to produce end‐of‐window fault probabilities. To ensure operational reliability, a lightweight per‐sensor eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) stage calibrates the LSTM score using window‐local statistics of the measurement. In this study, we investigate whether and to what extent fusing a physical model with sensor data improves fault detection, and whether per‐sensor threshold calibration matters. Our results indicated yes. The Area under the precision–recall curve (AUC‐PR) was improved by 3.7%–12.5% over the physics‐informed model compared to baseline non‐physics‐informed learning. In addition, post‐hoc calibration improved AUC‐PR by an additional 0.2%–2.3%. Across five cross‐validation folds, F1‐score (F1) increased from 0.75 for the non‐physics LSTM baseline to 0.83 with calibration, and further to 0.88 for the physics informed model. Adding post‐hoc calibration to the physics informed model yielded the best result at 0.90. The NPI is causal and auditable, exporting calibrated probabilities and binary alerts for direct operator use without retraining the LSTM, and offers a practical template for warning systems and training strategies that remain robust to unseen conditions.
